title: ax serve startup takes 4-5 seconds
[RFC] Universal Agent Harness Interface
body:
This issue is created for the sake of documentation for designing the harness interface.

# RFC

Authors: <authors>
Date: <date>
Status: <status>
Approvers: <approvers>
Reviewers: <reviewer
Workstream(s): <workstreams>
Self Link: <golink>
DO NOT EDIT ANYTHING ABOVE THIS LINE. SHARE EDIT ACCESS WITH HERMES-AUTOMATION@

# [AX] Universal Agent Harness Interface

Please refer to go/orcas-hermes-guide. Please submit your RFC at go/hermes-orcas 

## Summary

We are proposing a universal harness interface in Agent eXecutor(AX) which will allow users to bring their own agent implementations in an attempt to run large scale distributed agentic workloads on a  compute agnostic stack. AX is a distributed agent orchestration runtime that can run complex short/long agentic loops with distributed agents in a user friendly and efficient manner. 

## Motivation

With the proliferation of agents and implementations, we are seeing a Cambrian explosion in harness engineering. Building an agent is no longer the step change in effort it used to be. With the release of managed agents APIs at Google and outside, users will be able to customize and build agents tailored towards use case and context. However not all users will be able to use a full stack solution and will require federation of multiple components of the agentic engineering stack.

The Agent Executor (AX) platform coordinates complex multi-agent planning, tool execution, and conversational loops. A fundamental challenge in AX is heterogeneity: agents are written in different languages (e.g., Go, Python), run in different environments (local subprocesses, remote Kubernetes actor pods), and require different sandboxing boundaries. Due to this heterogeneity requirement, users need to define the harness implementation they want to use alone with the environment in which they want to run the agent. The harness and platform agnostic requirement is important to stay relevant in the current fast changing industry where standards are being rewritten every day.

We will eventually provide Antigravity agents out of the box with support for connecting to GCP agent cloud services in a seamless fashion.  In addition to this, we will have support for some of the more popular agents being used in the industry today in consultation with our partners.

Harness = Agentic engineering stack surrounding the model (similar to a class)
Agent = Instance of the harness with specific prompts, SIs, tools and skills. (similar to an object)

## Proposal

The what and how of your proposal. Please add any pertaining documents that are needed for additional context including technical designs or PRDs

To maintain a clean, platform-agnostic orchestrator, the system must interact with all agents through a single, unified interface. The Universal Agent Harness Interface decouples the orchestrator from specific agent SDKs and environments, abstracting away lifecycle management, stream queuing, and resource reclamation.

The orchestrator is defined as that central coordination mechanism in AX. This is implemented as the Controller in AX. 
Note: With this redesign we are going to be using the name ControllerV2 to refer to the Controller. The legacy Controller will be replaced with this. 

Controller V2 (internal/controller2) acts as the single source of truth (SSOT) orchestrator for AX. It is built on five core structural principles:
1. Strict Decoupling (Harness Boundary): The controller never directly binds to specific agent SDKs. It interacts with workers solely through abstract Harness, Execution, and Handler boundaries.
2. Single-Writer Concurrency Control: Eliminates Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) races by queuing concurrent conversation runs in thread-safe FIFO queues per conversation. The client will handle any duplicate conversations initiated by the user. 
3. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) Enforcement: Protects client streams against durability inversion. Generated output blocks must commit to the database first before emitting downstream.
4. Request and Response messages are committed: All outgoing messages from the client are committed as STATE_PENDING. The append only execution log commits the response once received from the Harness with STATE_COMPLETED only upon successful turn completion. 
5. Cancellation-Safe Cleanups: Lifecycle teardowns use detached context scopes, ensuring remote sandboxes are reliably cleaned up even if clients disconnect mid-stream.

The core of the refactoring relies on three interfaces defined in internal/harness/harness.go and how harness.Handler callbacks are orchestrated by ControllerV2 to maintain state consistency.
ControllerV2 initializes a new Harness instance based on the list of registered agents as well as the execution handler. 

The ownership of the execution moves back and forth between AX and the user defined agentic loop. It is critical to distinguish who implements and who invokes each interface. The developer extending the platform does not implement the harness.Handler interface. That interface is implemented by the AX Controller. The custom harness simply invokes (consumes) the handler callbacks.

Custom Harness: Connects to the runtime environment, receives raw agent events, and forwards them to the controller by invoking the handler.
Handler: Listens to incoming events, enforces the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) to SQLite, and streams output chunks back to the client

The Queue object is owned by the User defined Execution implementation of the Execution interface below. Currently this leads to an odd control flow of calling Queue() and Run() on a set of inputs that could be made using a single call. 
The reason for having two separate calls is that the Controller will be managing multiple conversations with multiple queues (1:1 queue->agent). Given a conversation id, the controller should queue the user messages for the given queue. During Run(), we expect the user to use the queue buffer based on how the agent handles multiple requests. If the agent handles model steering, then the agentic loop can call Run() on the user message. If not, the harness implementation will continue to buffer the message.

We have a separate Harness and Execution interface since we anticipate supporting N executions of a given Harness implementation if we want to support best-of-N configurations. 

We will have bi-di queues between the client and Harness and furthermore between the Harness and any sandbox environments we have running. This will allow buffering and allow harnesses to process input in accordance with their implementation. 

The controller is a process that is a Multi-Tenant replica set which will allow us guarantees of reliability from a single point of failure.

```go
// Package harness defines a common execution boundary and lifecycle hooks
// for interacting with agents, planners, or external gRPC services.
package harness

import (
	"context"
	"github.com/google/ax/proto"
)

// Handler defines the streaming event hook callbacks for an execution turn.
type Handler interface {
	// OnMessage is invoked when the agent generates output content during its turn.
	OnMessage(ctx context.Context, execID string, msg *proto.Message) error

	// OnComplete is invoked when the agent finishes its current execution turn.
	OnComplete(ctx context.Context, execID string) error
}

// Harness represents a service capable of starting execution sessions.
type Harness interface {
	// Start initializes a new Execution session for a conversation.
	Start(ctx context.Context, conversationID string) (Execution, error)
}

// Execution represents an active interactive session with an agent
type Execution interface {
	// Run executes the session and streams events to the provided Handler.
	// It blocks until the current turn completes or fails.
	Run(ctx context.Context, handler Handler) error

	// Queue enqueues new input messages to be processed in the next turn.
	Queue(ctx context.Context, msg ...*proto.Message) error

	// ID returns the unique execution session ID.
	ID() string

	// Close cleanly releases all resources associated with the execution session.
	Close(ctx context.Context) error
}
```

## Implementing a Custom Harness Extension

To register an agent and implement a harness, developers must implement the core interfaces mentioned above namely the Harness interface and the Execution interface detailed here: internal/harness/harness.go.
1. Implement the harness.Harness Interface:
    Start(ctx context.Context, conversationID string) (Execution, error):
    -> Initializes the execution session and must handle any pre-flight resource allocation (e.g., spawning local subprocesses, calling Kubernetes APIs, preparing tmpfs credentials mounts) and return an active Execution object.

2. Implement the harness.Execution Interface:
     ID() string: 
     -> Returns the unique execution turn UUID generated for the session.
    
  Queue(ctx context.Context, msg ...proto.Message) error:
     -> Buffers incoming messages in a thread-safe manner to support concurrent asynchronous prompts.

     Run(ctx context.Context, handler Handler) error:
     -> Spawns the agentic loop.
     ->: Establishes the bidirectional connection to the agent runtime 
     ->Flushes the buffered inputs over the stream depending on how the agent handles multiple requests
     -> Intercepts streamed messages from the worker, immediately passing each message to handler.OnMessage().
     -> Signals turn completion by returning nil or calling handler.OnComplete().
    
   Close(ctx context.Context) error: 
   -> Releases session resources to guarantee remote actor pods or child processes are cleanly suspended or terminated even on client connection disruptions.
   TODO: How should detached context scopes be enabled for cleanups?

## Case Study: Antigravity Local Run Mode Implementation

The google-antigravity SDK implementation in python/antigravity/harness_server.py and internal/harness/antigravity.go is a concrete example of a stateless design:

1. Request Ingestion: During Connect(), the Python gRPC servicer receives a list of historical messages and a new query:

```python
historical_messages = request.start.messages[:-1]
latest_query_text = request.start.messages[-1].content.text.text
```

2. Dynamic Step Hydration: The server runs hydrate_ax_history_to_steps(), translating Go protobuf messages into Python SDK Step structures (e.g., thoughts, text chunks, tool call schemas) and appending them directly to the conversation's internal step stack:

```python
history_steps = hydrate_ax_history_to_steps(historical_messages)
conversation._steps.extend(history_steps)
```

3. Execution & Cleanup: The planning loop runs conversation.chat(latest_query_text) and streams tokens back. Once the turn completes, the Python container/process is suspended.

4. The Harness is the SSOT where all the state of the execution is stored. This is a substrate actor which is snapshotted. We will provide a way for the user to access the artifacts that are created by the harness when executing a user request. 

4. We are also looking at local vs remote tool execution to be a harness implementation decision more than anything. 

## Architecture Diagram

The integration bridges the Go-based AX Controller with the Python agent sandbox:

[Go CLI (ax exec)] ---> [Controller V2]
                            |
                     (Registry Lookup)
                            |
                   [AntigravityHarness] (internal/harness/antigravity.go)
                            |
                    (gRPC TCP Dial)
                            |
                 [gRPC Harness Server] (python/antigravity/harness_server.py)
                            |
                (Dynamic Module Import)
                            |
               [Antigravity Agent Config] (examples/antigravity_agent/agent.py)
                            |
                     (google-antigravity SDK)

## Component Deep-Dive

### Go Client Adapter (internal/harness/antigravity.go)

The Go harness client bridges the ControllerV2 interfaces to the Python loopback service:

Harness & Execution Instances: AntigravityHarness satisfies the orchestrator's Harness interface. When Start() is invoked, it instantiates an antigravityExecution session tracking the unique execution ID.

gRPC Dialing: The Run method establishes an insecure connection via grpc.DialContext to the target address (defaulting to localhost:50053).
 
Message Delivery: Queued historical messages plus the latest turn messages are sent via AgentRequest to the Python gRPC daemon using the Connect method.

Streaming Reader: A loop receives streamed AgentResponse frames and routes them back via callbacks:
  - AgentResponse_Outputs: Triggers handler.OnMessage().
  - AgentResponse_End: Triggers handler.OnComplete().

### Python gRPC Daemon (python/antigravity/harness_server.py)

A lightweight gRPC server executing the ax.AgentService service contract:
 
Dynamic Agent Loading: Exposes a --agent_file flag to import the agent configuration dynamically (e.g. examples/antigravity_agent/agent.py), retrieving the global agent_config variable.

State Parity Hydration: To support stateless harness operations, the hydrate_ax_history_to_steps function reconstructs the conversation steps memory on every turn:
  - Translates user messages to StepSource.USER.
  - Translates assistant or model messages to StepSource.MODEL.
  - Populates thinking blocks if thought content type summaries exist.
  - Prepends these hydrated steps to the conversation object so the agent has full historical context.

Stream Conversion: The Connect method captures Chunks yielded from the Antigravity SDK:
  - Text instances mapped to standard text messages.
  - Thought instances mapped to thought summaries.
  - ToolCall instances mapped to function calls (with Struct serialization of arguments).

### Antigravity Agent Configuration (examples/antigravity_agent/agent.py)

 Agent Setup: Configures a LocalAgentConfig detailing system instructions and the available tools list.

 Custom Python Tools: Contains local function declarations like get_weather(city).

 Dual Execution Modes: Exposes a strategy_factory for loading config, allowing developers to run local CLI debugging with python agent.py "prompt", or serving over gRPC when wrapped by harness_server.py.

## Local Loopback Deployment

To ensure rapid iteration, testing, and development, AX implements a Local Loopback mode. This allows the Python agent code to be executed in a local process and dialed directly over a TCP port without container overlays:

### Subprocess Daemon Execution

The Python agent daemon is launched in a local shell, wrapping the standard google-antigravity SDK and exposing a gRPC AgentService (or HarnessService) on port 50053 over loopback TCP:
```bash
PYTHONPATH=python:. .venv/bin/python -m python.antigravity.harness_server --agent_file examples/antigravity_agent/agent.py --port 50053
```

### Registry Binding

In the Go CLI entrypoints (e.g., cliutil_harness.go) or e2e test suites, AX registers the local gRPC loopback client adapter:

```go
import "github.com/google/ax/internal/harness"

// Register the loopback address mapping the "antigravity" Agent ID
reg.RegisterHarness("antigravity", harness.NewAntigravityHarness("localhost:50053"))
```

### 3.3.3 Transport & Bidirectional Execution

When ax exec initiates a prompt, the AntigravityHarness dials localhost:50053 over an insecure gRPC TCP channel:
1. Dials Address: Connects to the loopback daemon using:
 `grpc.DialContext(ctx, address, grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()))`.

2. Bidirectional Connection: Invokes `AgentService.Connect(ctx)` to establish the stream.

3. Outputs Emission: The local Python agent executes its planning turn, returning tool calls and thought streams which are intercepted by harness.Handler and processed by Controller V2 using standard WAL commitments.

## Harness Registry Implementation

To support dynamic agent selection, the configuration plane consolidates all agent and runtime declarations into a single unified registry.

### Unified Registry YAML Schema (ax.yaml)

The unified registry defines both remote long-lived agents and dynamically provisioned sandboxed actors under a single configuration tree:

```yaml
registry:
  # Remote long-lived agent endpoints
  remote_agents:
    - id: "medical-deep-researcher"
      name: "Medical Deep Research Agent"
      address: "localhost:50051"
      protocol: "axp" # Standard AX proto over gRPC
      metadata:
        tier: "production"

  # Dynamically provisioned Kubernetes sandbox actors (SubstrATE)
  substrate_agents:
    - id: "secure-python-interpreter"
      name: "Secure Python Code Sandbox"
      port: 50053
      namespace: "ax-sandboxes"
      template: "ax-python-harness-template"
      protocol: "axp"
      credential_env_propagation:
        - "GEMINI_API_KEY"
        - "DB_CONNECTION_STRING"

  # Dynamic local subprocess harnesses (configured in-place)
  local_harnesses:
    - id: "antigravity"
      name: "Antigravity Local Loopback Harness"
      command: ".venv/bin/python"
      args:
        - "-m"
        - "python.antigravity.harness_server"
        - "--port"
        - "50053"
      address: "localhost:50053"
      startup_timeout: "5s"
```

### Go Struct Mapping

The Go orchestrator unmarshals these declarations into a consolidated Registry configuration matching the YAML keys:

```go
type RegistryConfig struct {
	RemoteAgents    []RemoteAgentConfig    `yaml:"remote_agents,omitempty"`
	ColabAgents     []ColabAgentConfig     `yaml:"colab_agents,omitempty"`
	SubstrateAgents []SubstrateAgentConfig `yaml:"substrate_agents,omitempty"`
	LocalHarnesses  []LocalHarnessConfig   `yaml:"local_harnesses,omitempty"`
}

type LocalHarnessConfig struct {
	ID             string   `yaml:"id"`
	Name           string   `yaml:"name"`
	Command        string   `yaml:"command"`
	Args           []string `yaml:"args,omitempty"`
	Address        string   `yaml:"address"`
	StartupTimeout string   `yaml:"startup_timeout,omitempty"` // default: "5s"
}

type Registry struct {
	mu        sync.RWMutex
	harnesses map[string]harness.Harness
}

// RegisterHarness registers a harness factory constructor for a given Agent ID.
func (r *Registry) RegisterHarness(agentID string, h harness.Harness) {
	r.mu.Lock()
	defer r.mu.Unlock()
	r.harnesses[agentID] = h
}

// Harness retrieves the registered Harness implementation for a given Agent ID.
func (r *Registry) Harness(agentID string) (harness.Harness, error) {
	r.mu.RLock()
	defer r.mu.RUnlock()
	h, exists := r.harnesses[agentID]
	if !exists {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("no harness registered for agent ID: %s", agentID)
	}
	return h, nil
}
```

### Local Subprocess Lifecycle Management

To run configured local harnesses, the Go Registry management controller handles the daemon lifecycle dynamically on startup and teardown:

1. Daemon Spawning: On startup, for each config entry in local_harnesses, the Registry spawns the specified command with args as an OS subprocess (using Go's os/exec.CommandContext).
2. Standard Output Redirects: Subprocess stdout and stderr are piped directly to the ControllerV2 logging handlers for debugging parity.
3. Startup Health Probe: The registry runs a background loop trying to dial the harness's address via gRPC/TCP. If dialing fails continuously for the duration of the startup_timeout (e.g., 5 seconds), ControllerV2 triggers an error and halts execution.
4. Harness Registration: Once the loopback connection succeeds, the registry creates a NewAntigravityHarness(address) (or generic gRPCHarness) and registers it.
5. Teardown Reclamation: On server shutdown (Close()), the ControllerV2 triggers context cancellation, sending a SIGTERM followed by a SIGKILL to clean up all spawned child processes.

## Controller V2 Integration

### Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) & Handler Stream [Task 1.2]

When the agent runtime streams tokens back over HarnessService, the harness.Handler implementation inside Controller V2 intercepts them:

```go
func (h *harnessHandler) OnMessage(ctx context.Context, execID string, msg *proto.Message) error {
	// 1. Enforce Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
	event := &proto.ConversationEvent{
		ConversationId: h.conversationID,
		ExecId:         execID,
		Messages:       []*proto.Message{msg},
		State:          "STATE_PENDING", // Only for Requests
	}
	if _, err := h.eventLog.Append(ctx, event); err != nil {
		// Discontinue immediately on DB write failure to prevent client durability inversion
		return fmt.Errorf("WAL append failed: %w", err)
	}
```
```go
// 2. Stream downstream to the client only after WAL commit
	return h.clientStream.Send(msg)
}
```
We cannot return an error and discontinue on DB write for responses. We will need another API exposed by the harness to help query artifacts or only allow for resumption for conversations that have a request and response pairwise objects in the database. We need to ensure that there is no inconsistency between the harness and controller states.

### Turn Commitment (OnComplete) [Task 1.2]

Upon completion, the ControllerV2 appends another log with the given conversation_id with STATE_COMPLETED. This is to ensure that we have logged streaming responses and account for mid stream failure. 

### Resumption Protocol [WIP]

Open Questions:
Confirm exactly when and how log playback/resumption is triggered (e.g., is it done automatically during the harn.Start() bootstrap or handled on-demand by the Controller when initializing the conversation turn?)

### Thread-Safe Run Lock & Queue Protection [Task 1.1]

 Run Lock Registry: Controller V2 maintains activeRuns map[string]string protected by a sync.Mutex to ensure only one active writer turn operates on a conversation at any moment, eliminating TOCTOU data races.
 Thread-Safe Queuing: The concrete Execution implementation wraps all inputs in a mutex-guarded buffer (pending []proto.Message) so that concurrent writes during stream handshakes do not trigger memory slices races.

## State Management & Data Ownership

To maintain strict transactional integrity and prevent distributed state synchronization issues, AX employs a centralized state ownership model:

### Single Source of Truth (SSOT)

 Durable Storage: All messages, execution logs and completed trajectories are persisted inside a single local SQLite database running on the host machine of the AX Controller. The database location is configured via the YAML property eventlog.sqlite.filename.

State Ownership: 
Controller V2 has absolute and exclusive ownership of the database connection and the storage layer. 

Harness actors have absolute and exclusive ownership of the artifacts or state home directory that is created as part of the execution. This is where the harness stores all the state and context required for executing the agent. The environment actor where we execute certain functions and the output is streamed to the Harness actor.

We need a mechanism for the client to be able to access the state of the distributed execution in AX as well as the state/artifact that is maintained by the Harness actor. The user should see no discernable difference between local and remote execution.

### State Mutation Lifecycle (Single-Writer Model)

1. Agent Egress: As the agent inside the sandbox container computes thoughts or calls tools, it streams the raw events over the HarnessService connection.
2. Controller Capture: The harness.Handler.OnMessage() callback in the controller intercepts the stream.
3. Serialized Database Writes: The Controller's single-writer thread serializes all database insertions, appending events to conversation_log with state set to STATE_PENDING (Write-Ahead Logging).
4. Client Forwarding: Only after SQLite commits the write transaction are the events streamed back to the client interface.
In events of DB failures, the client may not see the completed message. We will need to hydrate the controller database using the Harness actor state/artifact directory that is mounted per actor.  
5. Final Turn Commit: Upon turn completion, the Controller executes a final commit, with the conversation_id being set to STATE_COMPLETED

### Resumption & Replay Memory

Because agents do not manage memory across sessions:
When a conversation is resumed, the Controller retrieves all historical events marked as STATE_COMPLETED for that conversation_id. It unmarshals the historical messages for the last request/response message and injects them back into the agent's input buffer during the harness stream handshake. This restores the agent's context and memory without requiring database connections or file mounts within the sandbox itself.

## Remote Sandbox Actor Implementation (SubstrATE API Orchestration)

To support remote multi-tenant sandboxed execution, AX coordinates with the SubstrATE Kubernetes actor plane. The SubstrATE harness orchestrates sandbox lifecycles and gRPC routing through three primary API endpoints:

### Control Plane Client (ate.Client)

The AX Controller communicates with SubstrATE using a JSON-RPC client interface:

 CreateActor(ctx, conversationID, template, envProps) (ActorInfo, error): 
  ->Provisions a secure sandbox container inside the cluster for the conversation
template: Specifies the pre-registered Kubernetes container image configuration (e.g., ax-python-harness-template).
 envProps: Transmits dynamic credentials (such as GEMINI_API_KEY) to be dynamically mounted inside the pod.
   
Returns ActorInfo containing the dynamic internal pod IP allocated by Kubernetes).
 
SuspendActor(ctx, conversationID) error:
-> Suspends the sandbox container to release cluster CPU/RAM scheduling slots while keeping the underlying filesystem overlay volumes intact for future resumption.
-> DestroyActor(ctx, conversationID) error:
 
Completely deletes the container sandbox and purges all local workspace modifications and cached volumes.

### Container Daemon & HarnessService

Every provisioned sandbox pod container executes a lightweight, pre-baked Harness Daemon listening on TCP port 50053: The daemon exposes the gRPC HarnessService (with the Connect stream endpoint).
 When dialed, the daemon establishes a bidirectional stream with ControllerV2.  It unmarshals incoming HarnessMessage queries, passes them to the local agent, captures the agent’s streaming output chunks, and yields them back over the gRPC stream.

## End-to-End Execution Walkthrough (User Request via ax exec)

This section details how a prompt initiated by a user via the ax exec command is processed, routed, and executed by Controller V2.

### Chronological Flow

1. Client Request Initialization: The user executes ax exec targeting an agent (e.g., secure-python-interpreter). The CLI creates a proto.ExecRequest with the conversation ID, input messages, and the last_seq tracking number for synchronization.
2. Controller Handshake & Registry Lookup: The gRPC request lands at Controller2.Exec(). The Controller queries the Registry to fetch the appropriate constructor (harn, err := d.registry.Harness(req.AgentId)) and checks if an execution turn is already active for that conversation to enforce FIFO queuing.
3. Resumption & Sync Check: The Controller verifies if the client's last_seq matches the database. If a mismatch is found, it triggers the Resumption Protocol, replaying missing historical events from the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) to catch the client up before proceeding.
4. Harness Session Start (SubstrATE/Local): The Controller calls harn.Start(ctx, conversationID). For remote actors, the harness coordinates with the SubstrATE Control Plane (CreateActor) to provision a pod. For local agents, it dials the loopback port. This returns an Execution session.
5. Execution Queue & Run: The Controller invokes Execution.Queue() to buffer the user prompts in a thread-safe manner, followed immediately by Execution.Run(ctx, handler). This opens the bidirectional gRPC stream to the agent runtime daemon.
6. WAL-Enforced Turn Execution (OnMessage): As the agent yields tokens, the Controller's harness.Handler intercepts each packet via OnMessage(). It commits the event to the SQLite WAL as STATE_PENDING before streaming it downstream to the client to ensure durability.
7. Atomic Commitment (OnComplete): Upon successful stream completion, the Controller invokes handler.OnComplete(). This executes a single transaction to update all turn events to STATE_COMPLETED, providing a single source of truth for the conversation history.
8. Cancellation-Safe Teardown: The Controller executes Execution.Close() using a detached context (WithoutCancel). This ensures that even if the user disconnects, remote actors are suspended or subprocesses are reclaimed reliably.
   The controller fetches the registered harness constructor: harn, err := d.registry.Harness(req.AgentId).

4. Harness Session Start:
   The controller calls harn.Start(ctx, req.ConversationId):
    For a remote SubstrATE actor, the harness calls the Kubernetes control APIs (CreateActor) to allocate or wake up a sandboxed pod container, receives the dynamic pod IP, and dials the gRPC endpoint on port 50053.
    For a local agent, it dials the loopback port of the active agent process.
    Returns a concrete Execution session wrapping the gRPC connection.

5. Harness Connection & Run:
   The controller calls Execution.Queue(ctx, req.Inputs...) followed by Execution.Run(ctx, handler). 
    Sequentiality Guarantee: While Queue() and Run() are decoupled in the interface to support flexible asynchronous inputs, they are always executed together sequentially in a single unified block during any active conversational turn (e.g., inside ax exec). The controller first calls Queue() to stage the user prompts, and immediately follows by calling Run() to boot the stream connection.
    Stream Connection: The execution session opens a bidirectional gRPC stream HarnessService.Connect(ctx), flushes the inputs over the stream, and closes the outbound direction (CloseSend), signaling the agent to begin processing.

6. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) Turn Execution [Task 1.2]:
   As the worker streams events back, the controller's harness.Handler intercepts each packet.
    WAL Enforcement: The handler writes the event to SQLite first as STATE_PENDING.
    Pipeline Emission: Only after successful SQLite commit is the event emitted over the client-facing gRPC response stream.

7. Atomic Commitment [Task 1.2]:
   Upon successful stream EOF, the execution loop updates all STATE_PENDING events for the turn to STATE_COMPLETED in a single SQLite transaction and triggers Handler.OnComplete().

8. Cancellation-Safe Teardown [Task 2.2]:
   The deferred Execution.Close() runs under a detached, timeout-bounded context (context.WithoutCancel(ctx)), ensuring the remote pod suspension or subprocess cleanup completes reliably even if the client disconnected mid-stream.

title: Harden Antigravity Interactions harness HTTP client
body:
Fix a substrate suspend/resume failure and tighten the config surface:

- Disable HTTP keep-alives on the harness's default client. On substrate the actor is suspended after a turn and resumed for the next (with a new routable IP), which leaves any pooled keep-alive connection stale; reusing it made the next turn's request fail. title: Surface server error events in Antigravity Interactions harness
body:
parseStreamedTurn only handled interaction.* and step.* SSE events; a server-emitted "error" event fell through the switch and was silently dropped. The turn then returned as completed-but-empty, which:

  - made a failure (e.g. INVALID_ARGUMENT for a malformed client tool result) look like a blank "no response" turn, and
  - persisted the failing interaction's id as a poisoned resume cursor.

Add an "error" case that returns a real error, plus a serverErrorMessage helper that extracts message/status from the error payload. Now a turn-level server failure aborts the turn with a descriptive error instead of being hidden.

Adds tests for the error-event path and serverErrorMessage formatting.

title: Replace Antigravity sidecar in-memory Agent cache with SDK-native resume
body:
## Problem

Antigravity harness caches Agent per conversation in memory. Substrate snapshot won't include memory, and local server restarts when a conversation resumes. This setup doesn't work for conversation
resumption.

## Assumption 

1. Single writer so no lock needed 

## Fix

1. Delete the cache. 
3. Use `LocalAgentConfig`'s native `(conversation_id,save_dir)` — SDK persists trajectory state to
`{save_dir}/{sdk_conv_id}.db`. 
4. **Note:** Each AX conversation gets its own directory under `~/.ax/antigravity/conversations/{ax_conv_id}/`; on
subsequent turns we discover the SDK's hash-id from the `.db` filename
and pass it back to resume.

**This is because SDK's `conversation_id` is resume-only — passing a non-existent id errors.** Hence discover-then-pass, not pass-always. 

Alternatively we can store the {AX convs_id : AGY convs_id} separately but this simplify the overall logic and setup 

## Next

`save_dir` is hardcoded here. Should be injected by controller via `harness_config` — see #269, #203. TODO in code.

- [x] Test local (`ax exec --conversation <id>` across fresh sidecar
      processes → resume works, isolation works)
- [x] Test substrate

title: Resuming a conversation failed with mismatched default harness value
body:
Currently, the controller registers the harness from ax.yaml, and mark one of them as default. When run `ax exec` without `--harness`, the default harness is used.

However, the default harness is not resolved throughout the code path. E.g., in the request and log, the harnessID is still empty string "". This caused some harnessID check failure when continues a conversation with CLI. E.g,
In the first run:
```
ax exec --server localhost:8494 --harness antigravity
```

title: ax dashboard reads only the SQLite event log and ignores Postgres configuration
body:
### What

`ax dashboard` always opens the SQLite event log and has no Postgres code path. When the controller is configured to use a Postgres event log (`eventlog.postgres.dsn` / `AX_EVENTLOG_DSN`), the dashboard does not read it and shows no data.

### Where

`cmd/ax/dashboard.go` (`runDashboard`):

- Reads `cfg.EventLog.SQLiteConfig.Filename` unconditionally (`dashboard.go:76`)
- Opens the DB with `sql.Open("sqlite", dbPath)` (`dashboard.go:83`)
- Runs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ...` on that SQLite handle (`dashboard.go:95+`)

There is no branch that inspects `cfg.EventLog.Postgres`, unlike `ax serve`, which supports Postgres via `eventlog.postgres.dsn`.

### Impact

For a Postgres-backed deployment, `ax dashboard`:
- ignores the configured Postgres DSN,
- opens/creates an empty SQLite database at the (possibly empty/default) `SQLiteConfig.Filename`,
- silently renders an empty conversations/executions list,

with no error indicating the store mismatch.

### Repro

1. Configure `ax.yaml` with a Postgres event log:
   ```yaml
   eventlog:
     postgres:
       dsn: ${AX_EVENTLOG_DSN}
   ```
2. Run the server and create a conversation (`ax serve` + `ax exec --server ...`).
3. Run `ax dashboard --config ax.yaml`.
4. The dashboard is empty; the Postgres data is never read.

### Expected

Either:
- `ax dashboard` reads the same event log backend as `ax serve` (i.e. support Postgres), or
- it fails fast with a clear error when a non-SQLite event log is configured, instead of silently opening an empty SQLite DB.

### Notes

Appears to be a known limitation. Filing to track adding Postgres support (or an explicit guard/error).

title: Design intent question: is per-turn actor suspension the intended granularity, or is idle-based / configurable suspension on the table?
body:
## Context

We're **evaluating AX + Agent Substrate** (self-hosted on Kubernetes, the recommended production path) as the runtime for coding agents. What drew us here is exactly the density story: we want a **small fleet of machines to serve the coding-agent needs of a large number of users**, and AX + Substrate's suspend/resume model looks like a great fit for that — an idle user's actor gives its worker back, so a handful of nodes can back many more users than they could concurrently host. That part is very appealing.

Our workload is **mixed**: both *interactive* (a user chatting with a coding agent, one message = one turn, and they're actively waiting on the reply) and *asynchronous* (scheduled tasks where nobody is watching and only the final result matters).

Everything below is a **design-intent question**, not a bug report — we want to understand whether the current lifecycle behavior is the intended design point before we build anything around it, so we don't fork or fight the framework.

## What we observe

On the Substrate harness, each turn ends with `substrateExecution.Close()` unconditionally calling `SuspendActor` (external snapshot), and the next turn begins with `ResumeActor`. So **every single turn closes the actor**, and the next one has to resume it — even in an active session where the user sends the next message a second or two later.

For our async tasks this is exactly right, and it's the density win we came for — an actor that finishes and sits idle for minutes/hours *should* release its worker. The friction shows up in the interactive path: for **short tasks where a person is right there waiting to drive the next turn**, closing the actor after every turn and resuming it on the next makes the back-and-forth feel slow, because each reply pays a fresh resume before it can start. (We're still segmenting the exact breakdown on our side — this issue is about the *design intent*, not asking you to explain our numbers.)

## The question

Reading the README **History** section, the stated rationale for suspend/resume is long idle periods:

> *"An agent might compute intensively for a minute, then sit idle for **hours or days** awaiting human approval. Keeping a stateful actor active during these long idle periods is highly inefficient and cost-prohibitive at scale."*

That rationale (avoid keeping actors warm during *long* idle) makes complete sense to us. What we'd like to understand is the **granularity**:

1. **Is per-turn suspension the intended design point**, or is it more of a current implementation choice in the Substrate harness (`Close()` → `SuspendActor`) that happens to be the simplest correct behavior? The README motivates suspension for "hours or days" of idleness, but the implementation suspends at the seconds-scale gap between consecutive turns in an active session too.

2. **Is there any intent to make suspension policy idle-aware or configurable** — e.g. keep an actor warm while a session is actively producing turns, and only suspend after a configurable idle threshold (which would still aggressively suspend the long-idle / awaiting-approval case the README targets, and the async case, while avoiding churn during active back-and-forth)? We'd envision this as an opt-in knob owned by the deployer, consistent with AX being self-hosted and *"not a managed service."*

3. Related, is `PauseActor` (node-local snapshot / warm resume, as opposed to `SuspendActor`'s external snapshot) considered part of the intended lifecycle toolkit for the "briefly idle but likely-to-continue" case, or is external suspend the only sanctioned path today?

## Relationship to existing work

We see **#268 (Integrate DurableDir)** aimed at improving resumption performance, and the roadmap item *"Improvements to resumption protocols."* We read the official direction for latency as **making resume cheaper** rather than suspending less often — is that a fair reading? Even with a much cheaper resume, an active interactive session still pays the per-turn round-trip (new routable IP each turn, connection pools going stale — cf. the keep-alive workaround in #285, snapshot I/O). An idle-aware policy would remove that fixed cost during active sessions in a way cheaper-resume alone cannot. We'd like to understand how you see these two levers relating.

We'd really appreciate your read on whether idle-aware / configurable suspension is compatible with AX's goals, or whether per-turn suspend is a deliberate, load-bearing invariant we should design around instead. Happy to share our segmented latency measurements once we have them if that's useful input. Thanks!

title: antigravity interactions harness - improve TTFT (per-turn -> per chunk streaming)

## Problem statement

The Antigravity **Interactions** harness's output granularity is **per turn**, coarser than the SDK harness (which is per-Content / block).


## Code pointers 

- Buffer text deltas into one string: https://github.com/google/ax/blob/6c6bf181062d3e336fa209f4ac4dc6258d02c219/internal/harness/antigravityinteractions/antigravityinteractions.go#L921-L933

title: Questions about Google AX architecture, use cases, and scalability
body:
Hi team,

I have a few questions about Google AX that I'd like to clarify before diving deeper. Would appreciate your insights!

1. Entry point of the agent service

What is the primary entry point of AX? Is it a user-facing conversational interface (like a chat UI), or is it an API/endpoint designed for external agents to call and interact with?

2. Multi-agent platform scenario

The architecture seems to be designed around the idea that a large number of agent services run on a single platform. However, from what I've observed, this doesn't seem to be a common use case in production today.

Could you share more about the typical user scenarios or real-world use cases that drive this requirement? Is this more of a forward-looking vision, or are there already production workloads that demand this kind of large-scale agent orchestration?

3. AX: Agent or Agent Runtime?

The AX framework itself includes components like a Planner, LLM, and Executor, which makes it look very much like an agent. At the same time, it also acts as a runtime for orchestrating other agents.

So, is AX intended to be an actual agent that performs tasks itself, or is it primarily an agent runtime/framework that provides infrastructure for other agents to run on top of? A clear distinction here would be very helpful.

4. Scalability concern: Is the Planner a bottleneck under high concurrency?

In a high-concurrency scenario with a large number of agents running simultaneously, all of them would presumably rely on the central Planner for task planning and orchestration. This seems like it could become a single point of contention and a performance bottleneck, especially given that planning often involves LLM inference with non-trivial latency.

Is the Planner designed to be horizontally scalable (e.g., running as a cluster with load balancing)? Or are there other mechanisms built into AX to address this scalability challenge?

Thanks in advance for your time and clarification. These questions will help us better understand whether AX fits our production use cases.

title: Controller ignores ExecRequest.last_seq: disconnected clients cannot replay missed events
body:
### Summary

The `ax exec --last-seq <n>` flag is accepted by the CLI and sent on the wire, but the controller never reads `ExecRequest.LastSeq`. A disconnected client that reconnects with `--last-seq` does **not** get the events it missed replayed; the field is silently ignored.

### Evidence

- Client sets it: `cmd/ax/exec.go` (`--last-seq` flag → `ExecRequest.LastSeq`).
- Proto field exists: `proto/ax.proto` (`int32 last_seq = 3;`).
- **No server-side reader**: `LastSeq` / `GetLastSeq()` has zero non-test references anywhere under `internal/` (including `internal/controller/`). `Controller.Exec` resumes purely from conversation `state` via `ResumptionState`, never filtering/replaying by sequence.

### Regression

Server-side `last_seq` handling used to exist:
- #202 renamed `last_seen_seq` → `last_seq`
- #262 "return error when requested last_seq is missing from event log" filtered events (`ev.Seq > req.LastSeq`) in `tryResuming`

The recent controller rewrite in #308 ("Handle default harness correctly") replaced `tryResuming`/`ResumptionState`, and the `last_seq` handling was dropped in the process.

### Impact

- Disconnect/reconnect replay is broken: a client that saw up to seq N and reconnects with `--last-seq N` still cannot backfill the events it missed while a conversation was in flight.
- The flag is effectively dead: it is documented and accepted but has no effect.

### Repro

1. Start a conversation and note the last `seq` printed.
2. Disconnect the client mid-execution.
3. Reconnect: `ax exec --conversation <id> --last-seq <n> --resume`.
4. Observe the missed events between `<n>` and the current head are not replayed.

### Expected

Either:
- Restore server-side `last_seq` handling so the controller replays events with `seq > last_seq` (as in #262), returning a clear error when `last_seq` is not in the event log; or
- If the field is intentionally deprecated, remove it from the CLI/proto and update docs.

### Notes

Docs corrected in #319 (README no longer promises the replay behavior) while this code gap is open. Related historical discussion: #7 (closed).

title: Antigravity SDK harness on substrate relies on an implicit sidecar default for save_dir instead of passing --state-dir
body:
### Summary

When the built-in Antigravity SDK harness runs via `ax harness antigravity` (the path used by the substrate ActorTemplate), the Python sidecar is launched with only `--host`/`--port` and **no `--state-dir`**. AX therefore does not explicitly own the per-conversation trajectory (`save_dir`) path in this path — it relies on the sidecar's own built-in default. The local path and the Interactions harness both pass the state dir explicitly; the SDK substrate path is the odd one out.

### Background: how `save_dir` is derived

The sidecar derives per-conversation `save_dir` from its `state_dir` base:

- `python/antigravity/harness_server.py:210` — `overrides["save_dir"] = str(self._state_dir / conversation_id)`
- `state_dir` comes from the `--state-dir` CLI arg (`harness_server.py:484`), defaulting to `~/.ax/antigravity/conversations` (`harness_server.py:485`).
- SDK-native resume then scans `{save_dir}/*.db` (`_existing_sdk_conv_id`, `harness_server.py:155-159`).

So whoever launches the sidecar should pass `--state-dir` to explicitly control trajectory storage.

### The gap

**Local path (correct):** `cmd/ax/internal/cliutil/cliutil.go:94-98` derives `antigravity.DefaultStateDir()` and passes it into `antigravity.New`, which forwards it to the sidecar as `--state-dir` (`internal/harness/antigravity/antigravity.go:82-84`).

**Substrate path (missing):** `cmd/ax/harness.go` `runAntigravityHarness` builds the sidecar args with only `--host` and `--port`:

```go
cfg := pythonsidecar.Config{
    Module: "python.antigravity.harness_server",
    Args: []string{
        "--host", harnessHost,
        "--port", strconv.Itoa(harnessPort),
    },
    ...
}
```

**Reference implementation:** the sibling `runAntigravityInteractionsHarness` (`cmd/ax/harness.go`) derives `antigravityinteractions.DefaultStateDir()` and passes it into the harness config, with the comment "AX owns the resume-cursor path ... derived internally". The SDK harness should do the equivalent.

### Why it matters (correctness / robustness, not a currently-broken path)

Note: today the container runs as root (no `USER` in `cmd/ax/Dockerfile`), so the Go `DefaultStateDir()` (`os.UserHomeDir()/.ax/...`) and the Python sidecar default (`pathlib.Path.home()/.ax/...`) both resolve to the same `/root/.ax/antigravity/conversations`. So on the default image the missing flag does not currently point trajectories at a different location.

The problem is that this correctness depends on the Go and Python sides **coincidentally computing the same default**:

- If the sidecar's built-in default changes, or the image adds a non-root `USER` (different `HOME`), or `AX_HARNESS_WORKDIR`/env differs between the launcher and the sidecar, the two sides silently diverge and SDK-native resume (which relies on `{save_dir}/*.db`) can break across actor Run/Restore and snapshotting.
- AX should own the path explicitly rather than rely on this implicit agreement — matching the local path and the Interactions harness.

### Proposed fix

In `runAntigravityHarness` (`cmd/ax/harness.go`), derive the state dir via `antigravity.DefaultStateDir()` and pass it to the sidecar as `--state-dir`, mirroring the local path and `runAntigravityInteractionsHarness`. Fixed in #322.

---
Surfaced during the v0.2.0 verification pass (tracking: #299).

title: Adopt native env-var credential support from google-antigravity 0.1.7 and remove the sidecar override
body:
## Background

The antigravity harness sidecar (`python/antigravity/harness_server.py`) currently carries a temporary override, `_vertex_kwargs_from_env()`, that reads the standard GenAI environment variables (`GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI` / `GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE` + `GOOGLE_CLOUD_{PROJECT,LOCATION}`) and threads them into `LocalAgentConfig` explicitly.

This override existed because older `google-antigravity` releases (through 0.1.5, which we pin) did **not** read those env vars natively: a user following the documented recipe (export env vars, construct a bare `LocalAgentConfig`) would fall through to the AI Studio path and hit a misleading `"A Gemini API key is required"` error instead of routing to Vertex.

The upstream SDK has since been fixed to read these env vars natively (`LocalAgentConfig.__init__` hydrates `vertex`; `VertexEndpoint` hydrates `project`/`location` via a `model_validator`). That fix shipped in **`google-antigravity==0.1.7`** (published 2026-07-16), verified present in the published wheel.

The override is now redundant and marked `TODO: remove once AGY reads these env vars natively`.

## Plan

Tracked as two small, sequenced PRs:

- [x] **PR 1 — Bump `google-antigravity` 0.1.5 → 0.1.7.** Just `python/antigravity/requirements.txt`. Independently valuable; with the override still present, behavior is unchanged (explicit kwargs from the override simply win, same result).
- [ ] **PR 2 — Remove the `_vertex_kwargs_from_env` override.** Depends on PR 1. Deletes the override + `VertexKwargs`, simplifies `_build_default_config()` to a bare `LocalAgentConfig(system_instructions=...)`, and updates `_has_credentials()` to read `GOOGLE_CLOUD_{PROJECT,LOCATION}` from env (the SDK now hydrates those onto the `VertexEndpoint`, not the `LocalAgentConfig`, so the startup precheck must consult env rather than `config.{project,location}`). Includes the corresponding `harness_server_test.py` updates.

Ordering matters: PR 1 must merge first. Removing the override while still pinned to 0.1.5 would regress to the original bug.

## Notes on the 0.1.5 → 0.1.7 jump

ax inherits both 0.1.6 and 0.1.7. Reviewed the SDK diff scoped to ax's surface (`Agent`, `AgentConfig`, `LocalAgentConfig`, `types.{Text,Thought,ToolCall}`, `conversation.chat`) — no breaking changes. New `LocalAgentConfig` params (`env`, `subagents`, `session_continuation_mode`) are additive/optional. `DEFAULT_IMAGE_GENERATION_MODEL` was renamed but ax doesn't reference it.

title: fix(antigravity): resume pending executions via empty-input continue (#190)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #190. `ax exec --resume` on a `STATE_PENDING` conversation (the harness died mid-turn) failed with `no input messages queued for execution turn`. The controller resumes by re-running the pending turn with **no new input**, but both the Go adapter and the Python sidecar rejected an empty payload.

This change lets the empty resume flow through so the harness continues the interrupted turn from its own persisted conversation state:

- **Go adapter** (`internal/harness/antigravity/antigravity.go`): drop the  empty-queue guard in `Run()`. 
- **Python sidecar** (`python/antigravity/harness_server.py`):  drop the empty input guard call `chat("")` to continue the  persisted conversation, instead of returning `STATE_FAILED`. 

## Why empty-input continue (not input replay)

1. Verified empirically against the Antigravity SDK : the SDK persists an interrupted turn's input in its `save_dir` DB, and an empty `chat("")` **continues that turn** from persisted state. So AX does not need to reconstruct/replay inputs. 

2. This follows the general principle: AX passes through and lets the harness/SDK
own conversation state.

## Scope

Only hndles resume/continue after an interrupted turn (the #190 case).

Any other resumption use cases including true mid-step crash recovery (continuing a half-finished turn without redoing work) still requires SDK checkpoint/reattach and is out of scope here and will be handled more systematically with next milestone 


---

## Manual E2E test case

**TLDR**  Reproduces #190 end-to-end: interrupt a real turn mid-stream (kill the live
`axharness` sidecar), then `ax exec --resume`. Before this change the resume
failed with `no input messages queued for execution turn`; after it, the
interrupted turn is continued to `STATE_COMPLETED`.

More details below or http://shortn/_MeaAYOZkFY 
 

### Setup


### 1. Start a turn, then kill the harness mid-stream

```bash
# Start a long turn in the background
./bin/ax exec --conversation demo190 --harness antigravity \
  --input "Remember the secret word ORCHID. Then write a very detailed 800-word essay about the history of gardens, one paragraph at a time, slowly." &

# Once it is streaming, kill the sidecar to simulate a mid-turn crash
kill -9 "$(pgrep -f 'python.antigravity.harness_server' | head -1)"
```

The client stream fails with an EOF, and the event log is left `PENDING`:

```
⏺ Remember the secret word ORCHID. Then write a very detailed 800-word essay ...
Error: error executing with local server: harness execution failed:
  gRPC harness streaming failure: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = error reading from server: EOF
```

```bash
# Inspect the event log — it ends at STATE_PENDING (an interrupted turn)
python3 -c "import sqlite3,glob,json; c=sqlite3.connect(glob.glob('eventlog/*.sqlite')[0]); [print('seq',s,json.loads(p)['state']) for s,p in c.execute('SELECT seq,payload FROM conversation_log ORDER BY seq')]"
# seq 1 STATE_PENDING
# seq 2 STATE_PENDING       <- last state is PENDING
```

### 2. Resume

```bash
./bin/ax exec --conversation demo190 --harness antigravity --resume
```

**Before this change:**

```
Error: error executing with local server: harness execution failed:
  no input messages queued for execution turn
```

**After this change** — the harness continues the interrupted turn (recalls the
secret and resumes the essay), and the conversation reaches `STATE_COMPLETED`:

```
Conversation: demo190

I have successfully recorded the secret word ORCHID ...
As requested, I will write the detailed 800-word historical essay one paragraph at a time.

### Paragraph 1: Ancient Beginnings and the Dawn of Cultivation
The story of the garden begins not as an aesthetic pursuit, but as a crucial survival strategy ...
seq=3
```

```bash
# Event log after resume
# seq 1 STATE_PENDING
# seq 2 STATE_PENDING
# seq 3 STATE_PENDING
# seq 4 STATE_COMPLETED     <- resumed turn completed
```

title: Remove the binary
interactions: make WorkDir authoritative for run_command
body:
The interactions harness executed run_command relative to the process's ambient working directory, which is not reliably the agent's workspace: with no Cwd argument the command ran wherever the process cwd happened to be, and a model-supplied Cwd (including "/") was honored blindly. As a result tool calls often ran from "/" instead of the configured workspace (#332).

Make the workspace directory authoritative in the executor rather than relying on ambient process state:

- Add AntigravityInteractionsConfig.WorkDir (defaults from AX_HARNESS_WORKDIR).
- run_command now resolves its directory via resolveRunDir: no Cwd -> WorkDir; relative Cwd -> joined under WorkDir; absolute Cwd -> honored as-is. Empty WorkDir preserves the previous process-cwd behavior.
- Add WorkspaceSystemInstruction to orient the agent about its working directory so it emits workspace-relative paths, and wire it in cmd/ax.

Fixes #332

title: Security: per-request harness_config overlay allows process spawn via mcp_servers
body:
## Problem

Per-request `harness_config` uses a 2-field blocklist and accepts any `LocalAgentConfig` field, including `mcp_servers`. That lets a client inject an MCP stdio `command` that the SDK spawns at agent start (pre-model, bypasses `run_command` policy) → arbitrary code execution. Default `ax serve` has no auth, so this is pre-auth from the network.

Follow-up to #301 / gap left in #194.

## Proposed fix

Allowlist only safe per-request fields (`model`, `system_instructions`, `response_schema`, `session_continuation_mode`); reject the rest.

**Branch:** https://github.com/qerogram/ax/tree/fix/harness-config-overlay-allowlist
**Diff:** https://github.com/google/ax/compare/main...qerogram:ax:fix/harness-config-overlay-allowlist

`make test` + `make test-python` (56 passed) on that branch.

Auth/TLS and other harnesses are out of scope for this change.

`ConversationService` is removed for now until we know what kind of data operations we want to provide for event log management.
